title.en: The Laywoman Who Read Minds and the Monk Who Fled Her
title.zh: 知他心念的優婆夷與逃跑的比丘

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Sixty monks took up the rains at the village of Matika, and the headman's mother, taught the meditation on the body's thirty-two parts, outstripped them all and read their thoughts, serving each the food he merely wished for. One monk, terrified that she would catch his least evil thought 'like a thief by the topknot,' fled to the Buddha, who bade him guard only his thoughts; tamed thoughts bring happiness, and fed on her wholesome food he soon won arahatship.
summary.zh: 六十位比丘在摩提迦村結夏，村長之母學得身念處，修行超前眾僧，能知他人心念，僧人一想吃什麼她便供什麼。一位比丘害怕生起惡念被她「如捉賊般揪住髮髻」，逃回佛陀處。佛教他唯守護其心，馴服的心帶來安樂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: At the foot of a mountain in Kosala lay the thickly settled village of Matika. Sixty monks who had received a meditation subject from the living Buddha asked the headman's mother to lodge them for the rains, and she built them a monastery, serving rice-porridge with every choice flavor. To keep free from anxiety the monks agreed never to stand or sit two together, meeting only at evening and at dawn; when she rang the bell, they assembled one by one, each from his own quarters. Seeing them come singly, she feared they had quarreled, and learning they were rehearsing the thirty-two constituent parts of the body to grasp decay and death, asked to be taught the same practice. She mastered it so well that she outstripped the monks, winning the Three Paths, the Four Powers, and the Higher Faculties.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Looking with supernatural vision she saw her 'sons' still bound in lust, hatred, and delusion, lacking only wholesome food; from that day she served whatever they thought of before they spoke it. Fed on such food their minds grew tranquil and all sixty attained arahatship. Back at Savatthi they praised their hostess, and one monk set out to seek her hospitality. She divined each wish before he formed it, sent him a sweeper, then sweetened water, then rich porridge, then dainties, until at last she came herself. When he pressed her to confess that she knew thoughts, she only said, 'Those who know not the thoughts of another do thus, my son.' The monk reasoned that one unconverted entertains both noble and ignoble thoughts, that a single evil thought would be caught 'like a thief by the topknot,' and fled to the Teacher, who told him that that was the very place to stay: guard your thoughts alone, for they are unruly and flighty. Sent back, he thought only of his thoughts, and she, seeing he had found a master, fed him till he too attained arahatship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 2 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Nephew Sangharakkhita and the Eight-Cubit Robe

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: A young monk named for his arahant uncle Sangharakkhita received two rain-robes and wished to give the finer to his preceptor, who twice refused it. Fanning the elder, the nephew built a whole lay future in his mind, selling the robe, buying a she-goat, winning a wife, and finally beating her with a stick, and struck the elder's head with his fan. Caught, he confessed; the Buddha taught that thoughts wander afar, bodiless, seeking a hiding-place, and only restraint frees one from Mara's bond.
summary.zh: 出家青年以其阿羅漢舅父僧護之名得名，得雨季衣二襲，欲將好的供養親教師，兩度被辭。他邊扇邊妄想：賣衣買母羊、娶妻生子、妻子摔死兒子便以杖擊其背，竟用扇擊打長老之頭。佛陀說心念飄遠、無形無體，唯有調伏方脫魔縛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Elder Sangharakkhita of Savatthi won arahatship a few days after ordination, and his youngest sister named her new-born son after him. When Nephew Sangharakkhita grew up he entered the Order under his uncle and kept the rains at a village monastery, receiving two robes, one of seven cubits, one of eight. He resolved to give the eight-cubit robe to his preceptor, and when the rains ended he reached Jetavana first, swept the elder's quarters, prepared his seat, fanned him, and laid the robe at his feet. 'I have a complete set of robes,' said the elder; 'you wear it yourself.' Though the nephew pressed the gift again and again, the elder would not accept it, and the young monk, fanning on, brooded that his kinsman since lay days would not even share his possessions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then a whole lay future unfolded in his mind: he would sell the eight-cubit robe, buy a she-goat, sell her kids till he had capital, fetch a wife, and name a son after his uncle. Journeying to visit the elder, he would ask for his son to carry; his wife would snatch the boy and, lacking strength, let him fall under the go-cart's wheels; and he would beat her with a stick. As the fancy concluded, he swung the palm-leaf fan down on the elder's head. The elder, who knew every thought that had passed, said quietly, 'You did not succeed in hitting the woman; but what has an old Elder done to deserve a beating?' The nephew, ruined in his own eyes, threw down the fan and ran, was caught by the novices, and brought before the Teacher. The Buddha bade him not be disturbed: the mind dwells on things far off, and thoughts wander afar, alone, bodiless, seeking a hiding-place; whoever restrains them is released from Mara's bond.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Cittahattha, Seven Times a Monk, Seven Times a Layman
title.zh: 質多哈達——七次出家七次還俗

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Hungry in the forest hunting a lost ox, a young farmer tasted the monks' leftover porridge and became a monk; grown fat on the Buddha's gain and honor he longed for home, and swung back and forth between monastery and house seven times. On the seventh return, seeing his pregnant wife asleep and snoring like a swollen corpse, he grasped impermanence, won stream-entry on the road, and this time won arahatship; the Buddha recalled his own six returns for the sake of half a pint of seed-beans.
summary.zh: 青年為尋牛入林，飢渴中吃了比丘的殘食而出家；因佛門飲食豐美又還俗，如是七進七出。第七次回家見孕妻酣睡如腫脹的死屍，頓悟無常，途中證初果，此次終得阿羅漢。佛陀自述過去世曾為半升豆種六度往返。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: A respectable youth of Savatthi went into the forest after a lost ox and, oppressed by hunger and thirst at midday, entered the monastery where the monks bade him take the rice-porridge and leftovers. He reasoned that no matter how hard a layman worked he never tasted such porridge, and asked to be received into the Order. Fed on the rich offerings that accrue to Buddhas, he soon grew fat and well-liking, and then thought it idle to live on alms-pilgrimage; home he went, languished at the farm work, became a monk again, fat again went home, and so swung six times, helping the monks each time he returned, so that they named him Cittahattha, Thought-controlled, for he lived under the sway of his thoughts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The seventh time, back from the forest with his farming implements, he stepped in to put on his yellow robe once more, and found his pregnant wife abed and asleep: undergarment fallen off, saliva at her mouth, snoring, mouth wide open, like a swollen corpse. Grasping that all in this world is transitory and involved in suffering, he cried that for her sake he had never been able to stand fast, and ran out binding the robe about his belly. His mother-in-law sneered to the sleeping wife that he would be back in a few days, but on the road, repeating 'All is transitory,' Cittahattha won the Fruit of Conversion. The monks refused him: 'Your head is like a grindstone.' Admitted once more because he had helped them, he attained arahatship within days; asked mockingly when he would leave this time, he answered he had put away attachment to the world and had no desire to go.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the monks reported that he had 'renounced both good and evil,' the Buddha confirmed that the passions are grievous beyond measure: could they take on form, a whole world would be too small to hold them. Even he, the Buddha said, all because of half a pint-pot of seed-beans and a blunt spade, became a monk six times and returned to the world six times. Long ago at Benares the ascetic Kuddala, the Spade Sage, kept leaving his hermitage to plant those beans; the seventh time he flung pot and spade into the Ganges with his eyes shut, whirling it thrice overhead so he could not see where it fell, and cried three times, 'I have conquered!' The king, fresh from victory over his enemy, came to contest the boast, and the sage answered that the king had conquered only bandits without, while he had conquered the bandit of desire within, and that victory alone is true which need not be won again. That Spade Sage was the Buddha himself, and the king with all his retinue became monks at his feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Monks, the Tree-Spirits, and the Weapon of Loving-Kindness
title.zh: 眾比丘、樹神與慈心之武器

region.en: Forest-grove a hundred leagues from Savatthi
region.zh: 距舍衛城百由旬之森林

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Five hundred monks who settled a forest-grove for the rains shamed its tree-spirits into vacating their tree-homes for two weeks, until the spirits drove them out with bodiless heads, headless trunks, and demon voices. Sent back by the Buddha armed with the Karaniya Metta Sutta, recited outside the hermitage, they turned the spirits into guards and well-wishers, and meditating that the body is fragile as a potter's jar, won insight while the Buddha, a hundred leagues away, appeared among them.
summary.zh: 五百比丘入林結夏，樹神因慚愧而攜眷下樹、席地而坐兩週，最後現無頭之身、無身之頭與惡鬼之聲驅僧。佛陀授以《慈經》為武器，令眾僧於林外誦經後入林；樹神轉為護衛，僧眾觀身如陶坯，於佛遙現中證悟。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Five hundred monks who had received a meditation subject from the Teacher went a hundred leagues to a large village and, invited by the inhabitants, took up residence in a nearby forest-grove. The virtuous spirits dwelling there came down from the trees at once, judging it improper to dwell with wife and children above monks, and sat on the ground expecting the visitors to leave in the morning. A fortnight they waited, then resolved to drive the monks away: in the night-quarters and day-quarters and at the ends of the cloisters the monks beheld bodiless heads and headless trunks and heard the voices of demons, while sneezing, coughing, and many ailments seized them. Frightened, they abandoned the grove and returned to the Teacher, who told them they must go back, but this time not without a weapon: the entire Metta Sutta, the discourse on loving-kindness, to be recited in unison outside the hermitage before entering.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the monks recited the Sutta and entered the grove, the spirits throughout the forest conceived friendly hearts, came out to meet them, begged to carry their bowls and robes, rubbed their hands and feet, posted strong guards on every side, and sat down beside them; not a demon's voice was heard. The monks' hearts grew tranquil, and fixing the thought of the body's decay and death, reflecting that by its fragile, unstable nature the body is like a potter's vessel, they developed insight. Though the Teacher sat a hundred leagues away in the Perfumed Chamber, he knew, sent forth a luminous image of himself, and appeared among them as if seated face to face, diffusing six-colored rays, confirming that the body is indeed like a potter's vessel. Attack Mara with the weapon of wisdom, he said, stand guard over him defeated, and never rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 3, story 6 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Vidudabha Wreaks Vengeance on the Sakyans

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: King Pasenadi, insulted by monks who stayed away when his mind wandered, was told a past life of the Buddha; to win their confidence he married the Sakya maiden Vasabhakhattiya, secretly a slave's daughter. Their son Vidudabha, discovering his mother's shame when a slave-girl washed his seat with milk and water, vowed to wash his throne in Sakyan blood: three times the Buddha turned his army back from a tree of scanty shade, saying the shade of his kinsmen kept him cool, but the fourth time past karma spoke, and Vidudabha massacred the clan, only to be drowned with his army in a river flood.
summary.zh: 波斯匿王因僧眾不再上門而生怨，佛陀說過去本事後，王娶釋種女葦莎縛吉底耶（實為婢女之女）以結親。其子毘琉璃王知母出身後發誓以釋迦族之血洗座。三度出征，佛陀坐於無蔭樹下阻之：「親族之蔭使我涼爽。」第四次業力難逃，釋族被屠，毘琉璃王及其軍亦被洪水捲入海中。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely. Contains the massacre of the Buddha's clan.

passages.text: King Pasenadi of Kosala resolved to feed the Congregation daily, but when distraction of mind made him neglect the serving on three days, the monks one by one stayed away, until only Ananda remained, guarding the king's house out of the merit of his hundred-thousand-cycle wish. Angry, the king complained to the Buddha, who recited the Sutta on the nine traits of families worth visiting, and told of the ascetic Kesava, who left a king who waited on him to rejoin pupils among whom he could eat with confidence: 'Confidence is the best flavor.' To win that confidence the king sent to the Sakyas for a maiden of the Buddha's kin. Mahanama, unwilling to give a true-born daughter to an enemy king, sent Vasabhakhattiya, his beautiful daughter by a slave-woman, and had her eat at one dish with him to deceive the messengers; Pasenadi sprinkled her chief consort.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vasabhakhattiya bore a golden-skinned son and always put off the boy's wish to visit his kinsmen. At sixteen he went to Kapilavatthu with a great retinue; the Sakyas, refusing to bow to a slave's son, sent their young princes to the country and showed him hospitality in the rest-house without one obeisance. After his departure a slave-woman, washing the seat where he had sat with milk and water, muttered contemptuously, 'This is the seat where sat the son of the slave-woman Vasabhakhattiya'; a soldier who had forgotten his sword overheard, and the army learned the truth. Vidudabha vowed, 'When I am established in my kingdom, I will wash my seat with the blood of their throats.' Pasenadi degraded mother and son until the Buddha, preaching the Kathvahana Jataka, restored them, and Pasenadi died in a rest-house at Rajagaha while his commander crowned Vidudabha in his absence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: As king, Vidudabha marched to slay the Sakyans. The Teacher went through the air to sit at the foot of a tree with scanty shade by the roadside, and Vidudabha bowed and turned back, and so a second and a third time; but knowing the Sakyans' former deed of casting poison into the river, and that karma cannot be averted, the Buddha went not a fourth time. The Sakyans, refusing to kill, spent their arrows flying between shields and ear-holes without wounding a man, then stood with blades of grass or reeds in their teeth, willing to die rather than lie; Vidudabha slew the rest, sparing not infants, and washed his seat with their blood. Mahanama drowned himself rather than eat with a slave's son, and was carried off by the Naga king. At the river Adravati a sudden flood carried Vidudabha and all his men out to sea as food for fishes and tortoises: even while a man is gathering flowers, death comes like a flood that overwhelms a sleeping village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 3 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Niggardly Kosiya and the Cakes That Never Ran Out
title.zh: 慳吝拘希亞與喫不完的煎餅

region.en: Town of Jaggery near Rajagaha; Jetavana
region.zh: 王舍城附近的蔗糖鎮、祇園精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The treasurer Kosiya of eighty crores would not spend a drop of oil, and craved a fried cake so fiercely that he bolted himself into the top of his seven-storied house to bake it with broken rice. The Buddha sent Moggallana, who stood at his window wreathed in smoke until the miser's craving broke; the couple were carried by a miracle staircase to Jetavana, fed the Buddha and five hundred monks from a basket of cakes that never diminished, and gave eighty crores away; a 'Cake-cave' marks the leftovers still.
summary.zh: 家有八億財卻滴油不施的長者拘希亞，思食煎餅成疾，躲上七層樓頂用碎米自煎。佛陀遣目犍連現於窗前，以煙熏迫其慳心瓦解，再以樓梯接至祇園精舍，其煎餅供五百僧而愈供愈多，餅盡傾於「餅窟」。長者從此廣行布施。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: In the town of Jaggery near Rajagaha lived the treasurer Niggardly Kosiya, master of eighty crores, who never gave or used so much as a drop of oil that would stand on a blade of grass, so that his wealth lay unused like a pool haunted by spirits. Seeing a countryman eat a sour-gruel cake on his way home from the palace, he was seized by hunger but would not say so, and grew yellow, veins standing out, lying on his bed hugging it. Only when his wife pressed him did he whisper his craving, and then pared the feast down step by step: not the town, not a street, not the household, not the family, until at last one cake for himself, made of broken rice on a potsherd, to be baked on the topmost floor of the seven-storied mansion, where he climbed bolting each door behind him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: That morning the Buddha sent Moggallana to overmaster the treasurer without impairing his faith or his riches. Poised in the air at the window, the elder walked, sat cross-legged, and stood on the sill while the miser snarled that none of it would get him anything; then the elder belched smoke until the whole mansion was one mass of it, and the treasurer, eyes stinging, bade his wife cook one little cake to get rid of him. The dough swelled past the pot; every cake exceeded the last; and when the wife tried to take one from the basket, all the cakes stuck together. Husband and wife pulled with might and main, sweat poured from him, and his craving vanished. The elder preached almsgiving to them, took the couple and the basket in hand, left the head of their staircase in Jaggery and set its foot at the battlemented gate of Jetavana, and in less time than walking downstairs the two stood before the Buddha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Teacher and five hundred monks ate their fill, the couple ate their fill, and still the cakes suffered no diminution until the leftovers were thrown into a cave near the gate, which is called the Cake-cave to this day. At the words of thanksgiving both husband and wife were established in stream-entry, and mounting the staircase at the gate they found themselves at home, free to spend eighty crores solely in the religion of the Buddha. When the monks praised Moggallana in the Hall of Truth, the Buddha declared that a monk must approach a household as a bee approaches a flower, gathering honey without hurting the bloom, its color, or its scent, and praised the elder in the stanza: even so should a sage go about a village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Visakha's Marriage and the Building of Pubbarama
title.zh: 毘舍佉成婚與東園鹿母講堂

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Crowned with the garland of the Five Beauties at a riverside festival, the merchant's daughter Visakha married into the heretic household of Migara, answered ten riddling admonitions from her father before the assembled householders, and converted her father-in-law, who took her breast in his mouth and adopted her as his mother. Her jeweled parure, touched by Ananda, was sold for nine crores and spent on the eastern monastery Pubbarama; at its festival she sang that her hundred-thousand-cycle wish was fulfilled.
summary.zh: 毘舍佉於河畔節慶中因五妙相被擲花鬘，嫁入外道米加拉家。公公無故逐她，她於眾長者前一一解釋父親的十條隱語訓誡，自證清白。米加拉聞法證果，以口含媳之乳認她為母。阿難尊者觸過的金蔓花鬘以九億金售予自己，建東園精舍（鹿母講堂）。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: At the Saketa festival called Public Day, Visakha, daughter of the treasurer Dhananjaya, walked unhurried through a sudden storm while her five hundred maidens ran; the Brahmans sent to find a wife for Migara's son reproached her as slothful, and she answered that a king, a state elephant, a monk, and a woman appear to no advantage running, and that a girl is a good for sale whose limbs must be kept whole. Observing her teeth, the Brahmans threw over her the golden garland worth a hundred thousand. Married to Punnavaddhana, she was accused by her father-in-law Migara, a patron of the Naked Ascetics, and bidden to prove herself before the assembled householders by explaining the Ten Admonitions her father had given with hidden meanings: the fire not to be carried out means never tell of a fault you find in husband or father-in-law; the fire not to be brought in means never repeat what neighbors say against them. Cleared of every charge, she won her one condition: that the congregation of monks might be fed in that house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Naked Ascetics surrounded the house and forbade Migara to come, he sat behind a curtain; but the Buddha declared that beyond curtain, wall, or mountain he could make his voice heard, and as Migara listened, his mind ripened, and he was established in stream-entry. Lifting the curtain, he went to his daughter-in-law and, taking her breast in his mouth, adopted her as his mother, 'To-day henceforth you are my mother'; and thenceforth she was called Mother of Migara. Later the parure worth nine crores that her grandfather's smiths had made was forgotten by her slave-girl and hung by Ananda beside the staircase; Visakha, who would wear nothing her master's hand had touched, could find no buyer rich enough, so she paid its price herself, nine crores more for the building, and nine crores of alms, and raised a thousand-roomed dwelling for the monks at the eastern gate, Pubbarama, with Moggallana fetching whole trees a hundred leagues.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the day the monastery was opened, Visakha walked the rounds with children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren, singing five stanzas: when shall I give the gift of a monastery? Fulfilled is my desire. The monks wondered if her bile was out of order or if she had gone mad, but the Teacher said she was breathing forth a solemn utterance, and told them her wish made a hundred thousand cycles ago under the Buddha Padumuttara, when she saw his chief benefactress standing as mother to him and asked how a woman might become thus beloved; seven days of alms, a prophecy, and lives of merit had brought her to this hour. Even so, said the Buddha, from a heap of flowers of many kinds a garland-maker makes many garlands: so a mortal should perform many good deeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 4, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Pandita, the Seven-Year-Old Novice Who Watched the Ditch-Diggers
title.zh: 般達聰穎沙彌——觀掘溝引水而悟

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: In a former life the poor man Mahaduggata worked all day to feed one monk, and the Buddha himself accepted his bowl while Sakka cooked, so that a rain of seven jewels filled his house; reborn as the merchant's son Pandita, he was ordained at seven and, on the road, watched ditch-diggers lead water, arrow-makers straighten reeds, and carpenters bend wood, and asked to turn back to strive for arahatship. Sakka stilled sun, moon, and birds for him, and while the Buddha questioned Sariputta about food the novice won arahatship in his preceptor's cell.
summary.zh: 窮人摩訶達嘎夫婦打工一天只為供一位比丘齋飯，佛陀親往應供，帝釋化作幫傭下廚，供畢天降七寶盈屋。其後生為般達（智慧之子），七歲出家。路上見掘溝引水、製箭者烤竹弄直、木匠彎木作輪，遂向和尚求回寺修行。帝釋令日月停空、四天王守衛，佛以四問絆住舍利弗，沙彌於房中證阿羅漢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: At Benares, when the Buddha Kassapa visited with twenty thousand monks, a solicitor of alms urged even the pauper Mahaduggata to pledge food for one monk. The poor man and his wife hired themselves out, he splitting wood, she pounding rice as if she were dancing, and earned five measures of rice; gathering curry leaves by the river, singing for joy, he earned four redfish from a fisherman besides. Sakka, whose throne grew hot, came disguised as a man-of-all-work and cooked the meal, and the Buddha, tender to the poor, placed his own bowl in Mahaduggata's hands while kings begged for it in vain. Sakka's porridge perfumed the whole city, and at a sign from him a rain of the seven kinds of jewels filled the house till the children had to be carried out; the king made Mahaduggata treasurer. Dying at last full of merit, he was reborn in the heaven world, and in the present dispensation was conceived in the house of a merchant of Savatthi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 6, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the day the child was conceived the household's dull and deaf grew wise, and he was named Pandita, Youth Wiseman. At seven he was ordained under the Elder Sariputta, and on the eighth day, walking with his preceptor, he saw by the road a ditch by which men lead water to their fields, arrow-makers heating reeds to straighten them, and carpenters fashioning spokes and rims from senseless logs. 'If they can lead and straighten things that have no reason, surely we who have reason can bring our minds under our own control and strive for arahatship.' He gave back bowl and robe to the amazed elder, asked that only the choicest redfish be brought him, and shut himself in his preceptor's cell. Sakka's throne grew hot again; he commanded the Four Great Kings to guard the four quarters, the moon-deity to hold back the moon, the sun-deity the sun, and stood himself at the door-rope, while the Buddha detained Sariputta on the steps with four questions about food, sensation, form, and contact.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 6, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: While those four questions were being answered the seven-year-old attained arahatship. Sariputta knocked, the novice came out, took the bowl, and fanned his teacher before eating his own breakfast 'like a freshly blossomed water-lily'; then the moon and sun were released, the Four Kings went home, and the sun vanished strangely from mid-heaven, to the monks' alarm. The Teacher told them what had passed: even a Buddha had left his place to stand guard over his son. Ditch-diggers lead the water, arrow-makers straighten their shafts, carpenters straighten the wood, and the wise control themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 6, story 5 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Patacara Bereft of All Her Family

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The beautiful daughter of a Savatthi merchant eloped with her page; in childbirth on the road her husband died of a snakebite, a hawk carried off one son, the river swept away the other, and a storm destroyed her parents' house so that all burned on one pyre. Naked and mad she roared her grief through the city until the Buddha restored her mind and taught that the tears shed through the round of existences outweigh the four oceans; meditating on spilled water she saw rise and fall and won arahatship.
summary.zh: 舍衛城富商之女私奔，途中產子時丈夫被毒蛇咬死；鷹抓走一子，河沖走另一子，風暴摧毀娘家，父母兄弟同日焚於一炬。她赤身瘋癲流浪街頭，佛陀令其復明心志，教以輪迴中流的淚多過四大海水；後以潑水觀生滅，證阿羅漢。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Patacara, daughter of a merchant worth four hundred millions, was kept on the top floor of a seven-storied palace and loved her own page. When her wedding day with a man of her own rank drew near she smeared her body with red powder, disheveled her hair, and slipped out among the slave-maidens with a water-pot, fleeing to her lover. They lived in a distant village where she pounded rice and drew water, reaping the fruit of her own sin. Twice pregnant, she set out for her parents' house against her husband's will; the first child was born in a clump of bushes by the road. On the second journey a storm burst out of season, and as her birth-pains began her husband climbed an ant-hill for brushwood; a poisonous snake slid out and bit him, and he fell dead where he stood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 8, story 12 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Through wind and rain she bore her second son crouched on the ground, and at dawn took the newborn on her hip, giving the elder boy her finger, and followed her husband's path. At the ant-hill she found his rigid purple body; at the river, swollen knee-deep by the night's rain, she left the older boy on the near bank and carried the younger across on a branch, then turned back for the first. Midstream a hawk, mistaking the child for meat, swooped; three times she screamed, too far to be heard, and the bird flew up with him. The older boy, thinking his mother called, fell into the water and was swept away. Coming on a man from Savatthi she asked after her family, and learned that the storm had leveled her father's seven-storied house, crushing merchant, wife, and son, whose bodies even now burned on one pyre, their smoke in sight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 8, story 12 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Instantly she went mad; her clothes fell off unheeded, and naked as at her birth she wandered the roads wailing that both sons were dead, her husband on the road, her mother, father, and brother burning on one pyre, while people yelled 'Crazy fool!' and pelted her with rubbish and clods. The Buddha, seeing one who a hundred thousand cycles ago had wished before the Buddha Padumuttara for preeminence among nuns versed in the Canon, said none but he could be her refuge, and bade her return to her right mind; modesty and shame returned at once, a man threw her his cloak, and she cast herself at the Teacher's feet. He told her she had wept over the loss of sons and dear ones more than the waters of the four oceans, that to one going to the world beyond neither sons nor kith can be a refuge, and she entered the Order. One day, watching water she spilled run a little way and vanish, once farther, once farther yet, she meditated on those who die in youth, in the prime of life, and in old age, and at the Buddha's word won arahatship with the supernormal powers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 8, story 12 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Novice Sankicca and the Five Hundred Thieves
title.zh: 僧伽羯吒沙彌與五百大盜

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Thirty monks who had vowed never to sleep two together were betrayed to five hundred forest thieves, who demanded a victim for their sacrifice to the wood-spirit. Each monk in turn, senior first, offered his life, but the novice Sankicca insisted on going; the ringleader's sword bent double and split like a palm-leaf on his shoulder, and the whole band begged to be ordained by the child they could not kill.
summary.zh: 三十位比丘曾互約不二人同處，卻被指認給五百林盜，盜賊欲殺一僧祭樹神。從上座起人人爭先赴死，最後沙彌僧伽羯吒執意前往。盜魁一刀劈下，刀彎如馬蹄葉、再劈裂如棕櫚葉，遂棄刀懺悔，五百盜眾求此七歲沙彌為其剃度。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Thirty monks under the Elder Sankicca's instruction had promised never to stand or sit two together, that each might tend his own meditation, assembling only at the bell. A traitor who had lived two months among them, planning to steal their robes, told a band of five hundred forest thieves where the monks lodged and that a human offering would speed their vow to the forest-spirit. Striking the bell, the ringleader asked for one monk for the sacrifice. The Chief Elder said the decision lay with the senior and offered his life first; the Junior Elder claimed the duty belonged to the junior; and so every one of the thirty, though not brothers of one mother, rose in order saying 'Let none but me go,' until the novice Sankicca silenced them: 'You remain here; I alone will go,' for he was Sariputta's novice and the monks would not bear the reproach of yielding him up.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 8, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: While the thieves whetted stakes and spread leaves the novice sat apart and entered a trance. The ringleader swung his sword on the boy's shoulder, but the blade bent double, edge striking edge; a second blow split it from hilt to tip like a palm-leaf. No one, the Commentary says, could have killed him then even by piling Mount Sineru on him. Flinging down the useless sword, the chief prostrated himself: men a thousand strong tremble at his band afar off, yet this boy's face shone bright as gold in a crucible. Rising from trance the novice preached that one rid of the corruptions regards existence as a burden laid on the head, whose fall brings joy, not fear, and recited that he who has destroyed the Eye of Existence puts death down like a burden. The chief resolved to become a monk under the boy, and all five hundred bowed and asked the same; with the blades of their own swords and arrows he shaved them, dyed their clothes with yellow earth, and led the five hundred new monks back to the Thirty, whose tears had kept them from their meditations.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 8, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.zh: 被咒術定身的獵戶鳩鳩陀彌多羅

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The hunter Kukkutamitta, finding no deer in his nets but the Buddha's footprint, drew his bow to kill the man he thought had freed his catch, and found himself rooted to the spot; his seven sons, drawn by the same bow, were frozen too, until their mother ran out crying, 'Do not kill my father.' Father-in-law and grandsons alike begged pardon, all fifteen were converted, and the Buddha taught that the hand without a wound may carry poison unharmed.
summary.zh: 獵戶鳩鳩陀彌多羅見網中無獸而有佛足印，誤以為有人放走獵物，張弓欲殺佛陀，卻被定在原地；七個兒子持弓趕來也一一被定。其妻趕到高喊「別殺我父親」，眾人方知是岳父，齊來懺悔。十五人皆得初果。無傷之手可以執毒而不受其害。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: A rich man's daughter at Rajagaha saw from her window the hunter Kukkutamitta driving in a cartload of venison and followed him out of the city in soiled clothes till he took her on his cart; her parents held a funeral feast for her as one dead. She bore him seven sons and married them off. One day the Buddha, seeing that the hunter, his seven sons, and their wives were ready for conversion, went to the place where the nets were spread, and left his footprint on a net before sitting down in the shade. Kukkutamitta, finding not one animal in five hundred snares and five hundred spears, reasoned that someone was freeing his catch, and when he came upon the Teacher, drew his bow to kill him. The Buddha let him draw but did not let him shoot: the hunter stood as if his ribs were shattered, arrow drawn, unable to loose or lower it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 9, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the sons came seeking their father and saw him standing enchanted, they took him for an enemy and drew their bows, and were likewise rooted to the spot. The mother, going out with the daughters-in-law, saw beyond the bows the Teacher, and screamed, 'Do not kill my father; do not kill my father!' Husband and sons understood at once what a wicked deed they had about to do, their hearts softened, and at the Teacher's permission they lowered their bows and begged pardon; all fifteen were established in the Fruit of Conversion, and the hunter gave up the taking of life. The monks wondered how a stream-enterer could have handed her husband bow and arrows all those years; the Buddha answered that she acted only to obey her husband's command, never thinking he would take life, for if a man's hand be free from wounds he may carry poison and it cannot harm him; no evil befalls him who does no evil. Their past merits as builders of the Buddha Kassapa's shrine, given not in coin but with their very selves, ripened now into this conversion.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 9, story 8 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Anathapindika and the Goddess of the Fourth Gate
title.zh: 給孤獨長者與第四門的守護神

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: The gate-goddess of Anathapindika's house could not endure the radiance of the Buddha and his monks and, finding her patron now poor, urged him to abandon his giving and rebuild his fortune. Driven from the house with her children, she found no shelter anywhere, and by Sakka's advice recovered fifty-four crores of the merchant's scattered wealth to atone; then the Teacher forgave her, teaching that the evildoer sees happiness until his deed ripens, and the good man sees evil until his does.
summary.zh: 給孤獨長者家第四門的守護神不堪佛陀僧眾威德，趁長者家道中落，夜半現身勸他停止布施、重理家業。被長者驅逐後無處棲身，依帝釋之計尋回五十四億失散之財贖罪，懺悔後蒙佛赦宥。惡人未熟果時見樂，善人未熟果時見苦。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Anathapindika, who had spent fifty-four crores on Jetavana alone, went three times a day to wait on the Teacher, never empty-handed: porridge in the morning, medicines after breakfast, perfumes and garments at evening. But eighteen crores lent to traders went unpaid, and eighteen crores buried by the river were swept into the sea, so that he grew gradually poor, giving as before but with bird-feed and sour gruel. The Teacher told him not to be disturbed: pure intention cannot give the Buddhas coarse food, and once, in the time of Velama, he had stirred all India with rich offerings and won not a single person to the Three Refuges. When the Teacher and his disciples entered the house, the goddess who dwelt above the fourth gate could not endure the intensity of their goodness, and resolved, now that the merchant was poor and would listen, to detach him from his allegiance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 9, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: By night she stood poised in the air in his chamber and warned him that he would soon lack food and clothing if he went on feeding 'the monk Gotama'; he must give up lavish giving and mind his business. 'Begone,' said the merchant; 'though a hundred thousand like you should try, you could not move me from my course.' Unable to withstand the word of a Noble Disciple, she left with her children, but found lodging nowhere; the city's tutelary deity and the Four Great Kings refused to plead for her, and Sakka, though he would not speak to the merchant, told her the way: recover the eighteen crores lent to the traders, the eighteen swept into the ocean, and a third eighteen without an owner, and fill the empty storerooms. She did all this, then stood radiant in the chamber, begging pardon as the blind, stupid goddess of the fourth gate. Anathapindika led her to the Teacher, where she fell upon her face, and the Buddha forgave her: even an evildoer sees happiness while his deed is unripe, and even a good man sees evil while his is unripe; when they ripen, each sees his own fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 9, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Kundadhana, the Monk Followed by a Phantom Woman
title.zh: 摳那達那——被幻影女子跟隨的比丘

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: From the day Kundadhana ordained, a female form followed him whom he alone could not see: villagers fed 'our female friend,' the king staked out his cell and saw her vanish upstairs, and the monks cried 'corrupt monk!' The Buddha traced it to a goddess who, in the dispensation of Kassapa, took a woman's form behind a monk and ruined his good name, and paid for it in Avici; he bade Kundadhana keep silence like a broken gong, for by silence he would win Nibbana.
summary.zh: 摳那達那尊者出家之日起，身後即有一女子身影隨行，唯他本人看不見：村人連他的「女朋友」也供養，國王埋伏其房前忽見忽失，僧眾罵他「破戒」。佛陀追溯：過去迦葉佛時，一位天神化作女身跟在比丘身後毀其名譽，因此墮阿鼻地獄一劫。佛令其如破鑼般默然，以寂靜證涅槃。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: From the day Elder Kundadhana became a monk a female form accompanied him wherever he went; he himself never saw her, but everybody else did, so that on his alms-round the villagers gave him one portion saying 'Reverend Sir, this is for you,' and another saying 'And this is for our female friend.' Long before, in the dispensation of Kassapa, the same being, then a goddess of the Thirty-three, had seen two companion-monks as close as brothers going together to the Hall of Discipline, and thought in her folly to part them. When one stepped into a thicket, she assumed the form of a woman and followed him out, arranging her hair and undergarment; the waiting monk saw, though the elder did not, and accused him. Though the goddess later confessed the trick to the accuser, the pair's friendship was broken, and for that deed the goddess was reborn in Avici and suffered through an interval between two Buddhas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: Reborn at last as a man of Savatthi, he ordained, and the phantom woman came with him, so that the monks asked Anathapindika and Visakha to expel the unchaste monk, then appealed to the king, who went by night to surround the elder's lodging. When Kundadhana stepped out, the king saw the woman behind him; upstairs, she was gone. Twice more the king made the elder step out and saw her appear and vanish, and concluded it must be a phantom; instead of expelling him he invited him to take his Four Requisites from the palace alone, to the monks' fury. Stung, Kundadhana retorted that they were the corrupt ones, consorting with women, and the monks reported him. The Teacher asked why he answered slander with slander when he had seen nothing, told him the whole past story, and bade him never again hold converse with the monks: make no sound, even as a brass plate shattered at the rim, for so you will attain Nibbana. Speak not harshly to anyone, for angry words bring trouble; silent as a broken gong, you have already reached Nibbana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 4 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death of Moggallana the Great

region.zh: 王舍城黑岩林、竹林精舍

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Heretics hired thieves to kill Moggallana, whose preaching of the fate of the dead in heaven and hell drew away their patrons. Twice he slipped through a keyhole and soared through the roof, but in the third month the force of an old deed held him: beaten and pounded to grains of rice, he gathered himself by meditation, flew to the Buddha to announce his Nibbana, and passed away at Black Rock. The Buddha told how, to please a faithless wife, he had once lured his own parents into a forest and beaten them to death.
summary.zh: 外道僱盜賊殺害目犍連，因其宣說天獄果報令信施流向佛門。尊者兩度穿鎖孔、破屋頂飛脫，第三個月宿業現前而受擒，被肢解捶骨至米粒。他以禪定裹身飛回向佛辭行，於黑岩林入滅。佛陀說其過去生為取悅妻子，誘父母入林而擊殺之。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely. Contains the violent death of a disciple and parricide.

passages.text: The heretics met together and agreed that all the rich offerings to the monk Gotama had come about through Moggallana the Great, who visited heaven and hell and told men on earth what deeds win such glory and what deeds win such torment. 'If we kill him, the gifts will fall to us.' They hired thieves with a thousand pieces of money and sent them to Black Rock. The elder, knowing his abode was surrounded, slipped out through the keyhole; the next day he broke through the circular peak of the house and soared into the air; month after month the thieves failed. But when the third month came the elder felt the compelling force of the evil deed he had done in a former existence, and made no attempt to escape. Caught at last, he was torn limb from limb and his bones pounded to grains of rice; then, swathing himself in meditation as with a cloth, he flew through the air to the Buddha, announced that he was about to pass into Nibbana, preached a last discourse, performed such miracles as Sariputta had shown, and passed away in Black Rock forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: The thieves, boasting over drink, betrayed themselves, and King Ajatasattu had five hundred heretics and five hundred thieves buried waist-deep in pits, burned, and plowed to bits. In the Hall of Truth the monks said Moggallana had met a death he did not deserve, but the Buddha answered that only in this life did it look undeserved: in exact conformity with his former deed. Once, a devoted son who served his parents with his own hands married a wife who could not bear the old people, and scattered clay and scum about the house to make them seem filthy. At last he told his blind parents there were kinsfolk who wished to see them, handed his father the reins in the deep forest, and, yelling like thieves, beat his mother and father to death. For that monstrous sin he burned in hell for numberless hundreds of thousands of years, and in a hundred successive existences was beaten and pounded to pieces in the same manner. Whosoever visits punishment on the offenseless, said the Teacher, quickly comes to one of ten evil states, and at the dissolution of the body goes to hell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 7 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Santati, the Adorned Minister Who Passed into Nibbana in the Air
title.zh: 珊達帝大臣——嚴飾而於空中入滅

texts.period: Pali commentary, c. 5th c. CE (Buddhaghosa-tradition); Burlingame translation 1921

source.work: Buddhist Legends (Dhammapada Commentary), trans. E. W. Burlingame, HOS 28/29/30

summary.en: Santati, given a week of royal pleasures and a dancing woman after pacifying the frontier, was drunk on the seventh day when the dancer died mid-performance before his eyes; his week of liquor vanished like a drop of water on a hot potsherd, he went to the Teacher, and at a single stanza won arahatship. Rising to seven palm-trees' height he rehearsed his merit as a dharma-crier under the Buddha Vipassi, then self-cremated in the air, and the Buddha declared even the adorned man a Brahman, a hermit, a monk.
summary.zh: 珊達帝大臣平亂凱旋，王賜七日之樂與舞伎。第七日酒醉觀舞，舞伎絕食七日炫技，忽然倒斃。他七日酒意如水滴落紅熱瓦上瞬間消失，向佛求皈，一偈之下證阿羅漢，升至七棵棕櫚之高處自述前世弘法功德，於空中自焚入滅，捨利如茉莉花落下。

sensitivity.note: Canonical commentary of a living tradition; retold freely.

passages.text: Santati returned from suppressing disorder on the frontier of King Pasenadi Kosala, and the delighted king gave him his kingdom for seven days and a woman who danced and sang. For seven days Santati steeped himself in liquor, and on the seventh rode the state elephant to the baths, adorned with every adornment, nodding a salute to the Teacher as they passed. The Buddha smiled and told Ananda that this very day the drunken sot, so adorned, would hear one stanza and attain arahatship, then pass into Nibbana seated seven palm-trees above the earth. Heretics and believers marked the words, the one to catch him in a lie, the other to see his glory. At the bathing-place the dancer, who had fasted seven days to show her grace, was cut through by knife-like pains in her belly as she performed, and died before his eyes with open mouth and open eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Look to the lady!' cried Santati. 'She is dead, master.' At those words the liquor of the whole week vanished like a drop of water on a red-hot potsherd, and overwhelmed with sorrow he went in the evening to the one man he knew could extinguish it. The Teacher told him that on countless occasions this woman had died in this very manner and he had wept tears more abundant than the four great oceans, and spoke of what is past, letting nothing lie before, and nothing between be grasped. At the stanza's end Santati attained arahatship with the supernormal powers; and since heretics stood ready to mock, the Teacher bade him rehearse his past merit, not on the ground but poised in the air. Santati rose palm-tree by palm-tree to the height of seven and, seated cross-legged, told how under the Buddha Vipassi, ninety-one cycles ago, he had gone about proclaiming the Three Jewels on foot, then on a horse, then a chariot, then on an elephant decked in jewels, for eighty thousand years, sandal fragrance diffusing from his body and lotus fragrance from his mouth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: As he finished, seated cross-legged in the air, he applied himself to meditation on the element of fire, entered trance, and passed straightway into Nibbana: flames burst from his body and consumed flesh and blood, and his relics floated down like jasmine flowers into a white cloth the Teacher spread. They were enshrined at a crossing of four highways, that reverence there might yield the populace much merit. When the monks debated whether one who died adorned and in state should be called hermit or Brahman, the Teacher declared he was both, and spoke the stanza: even though a man be richly adorned, if he walk in peace, quiet, subdued, restrained, and chaste, and injure no living being, that man is a Brahman, that man is a hermit, that man is a monk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dhammapada Commentary, Book 10, story 9 (Burlingame 1921); not verbatim.
